analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice payouts for pain and suffering while requiring insurers to cut doctors' premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by three House Democrats, never got a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap the money a malpractice victim can win for pain and suffering at $250,000 in 1975 dollars — about $878,000 by 2005, far higher than the flat $250,000 cap in most tort-reform bills. In exchange, it requires every malpractice insurer to pass at least half of its savings to doctors as lower premiums, subjects insurer rate hikes to state hearings, and creates a public database of doctors' disciplinary records and malpractice payouts that patients can search and add complaints to. It also imposes sanctions on meritless lawsuits, funds mediation programs to settle cases without trials, and builds a voluntary system for hospitals to report medical errors.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, who would likely pay less for malpractice insurance; patients, who would gain public access to each physician's disciplinary history and malpractice payouts and a way to track complaints; and hospitals, which would face capped awards and get a shielded channel for reporting medical errors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Doctors, hospitals, and patients seeking records

how_it_helps.text: Caps non-economic damages (pain and suffering) at $250,000 adjusted for inflation from 1975 — roughly $878,000 in 2005 — instead of a flat $250,000, and the cap disappears in any state whose medical board fails federal performance standards.

Requires every malpractice insurer to estimate its savings from the cap and dedicate at least half of that to cutting doctors' premiums, with annual reports to HHS and civil penalties up to $11,000 per violation for noncompliance.
Creates an interstate, public database of physicians' education, malpractice payouts, and disciplinary actions over the prior 10 years, where patients can file complaints and track their status.
Encourages states to require insurers to justify rate increases at administrative hearings, with standing for health care providers to challenge them.

Imposes mandatory sanctions, including contempt of court and fines, on lawyers who file meritless malpractice claims, and funds voluntary mediation programs so some disputes settle without litigation.
Establishes a voluntary patient-safety reporting system with legal privilege so providers can disclose medical errors without that evidence being used in lawsuits.

analysis.who_pays: Patients who are catastrophically injured, whose compensation for pain and suffering would be capped even when a jury awards more, and malpractice insurers and trial lawyers, who face new mandates and sanctions.

drawbacks.text: A patient permanently disabled by malpractice could no longer recover full jury-awarded compensation for pain and suffering; the bill applies the cap in aggregate across all responsible providers and counts recoveries finalized before enactment.
The premium-cut mandate is largely self-certified by the insurers themselves, with a maximum penalty of $11,000 per violation — a small amount for a large insurance company.
Medical errors reported to patient safety organizations would be privileged and unavailable in lawsuits, keeping some evidence of harm away from injured patients.
The mandatory-contempt regime for filings that turn out unsupported could make lawyers hesitant to take close-call cases, which tends to hit patients with the hardest-to-prove injuries first.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades the core tort-reform demand — a damages cap — for unusually strong consumer-side terms: insurers must actually pass savings to doctors, rate hikes face hearings, and patients get a public disciplinary database. The cap it offers is far above the flat $250,000 standard of the era. The main cost falls on a small group: patients with the most severe, non-economic injuries. Whether that trade is fair depends heavily on whether the self-certified premium cuts would have materialized, which the weak enforcement mechanism makes uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in May 2005 and then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee in June, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Baird, a Democrat, introduced the bill on May 26, 2005, with two Democratic cosponsors — Reps. James Moran and Dutch Ruppersberger.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees on the day of introduction, and to the Health Subcommittee on June 3, 2005.
No hearing, markup, or vote of any kind appears in the action history, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, malpractice insurers kept the status quo — no damages cap but also no premium-cut mandate or rate-increase hearings — while patients kept full jury compensation but got none of the promised transparency or safety-reporting systems.

for.name: Brian Baird
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set its terms: a moderate damages cap paired with mandatory insurer premium cuts, rate-increase hearings, and a public physician-discipline database.

for.name: James Moran and Dutch Ruppersberger
for.role: U.S. Representatives, VA-8 and MD-2; cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only support beyond the sponsor.

against.name: Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee (109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee or its Health Subcommittee for a hearing or markup after the June 2005 referral.

against.name: F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill, which was jointly referred to his committee and never considered.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and no roll calls or recorded opposition exist, so no partisan split can be measured; the bill simply never moved.

industries.note: The damages cap would shrink what insurers pay out in claims, but the bill forces them to return at least half the savings as lower doctor premiums and exposes their rate hikes to state hearings, with penalties for noncompliance. Their main gain comes directly out of injured patients' compensation, which is why the stance is mixed rather than aligned.

The cap lowers the value of malpractice cases and the mandatory-contempt regime penalizes lawyers for filings a court later finds unsupported, making hard-to-prove cases riskier to take. Their fortunes track their injured clients', who lose uncapped compensation under the same provisions.

They would face capped awards and likely lower insurance premiums, plus liability protection for good-faith reports to state medical boards — gains funded partly by capped compensation for injured patients. They also benefit from the bill's public-disclosure standards only if it passes.

The bill explicitly excludes drug and device makers from its liability reforms, so their product-liability exposure is untouched while other health care providers get a damages cap. They gain nothing new but avoid being swept into the cap.
